title: LEARN TO TAP DANCE | "Sing, Sing, Sing" | BEGINNER TAP DANCE TUTORIAL | Step-by-Step Instruction!

observation_window.sampling: provider default; not continuous motion capture

extraction.teacher_style: The instructor uses a friendly, encouraging tone and breaks down each tap step into clear, bite-sized components. She frequently uses repetition and side-by-side split screens to show both full body and close-up footwork.

lesson_structure.note: Introduction to the song and instructor.
Explanation of prerequisites and equipment needed.
Step-by-step breakdown of toe taps and toe drops.
Introduction and breakdown of step-heels and digs.

cues: Your heels never leave the ground
Five, six, double tap, double tap
Step heel dig, two step heels
metaphors: Rocking up onto the heels to tap the toes
common_mistakes: Feet being too wide or too close together
Not using the whole body and just tapping with the feet
Doing a touch heel instead of a step heel where weight transfers
safety: Try the steps in whatever shoes feel safe and comfortable to you

steps_taught.name: Step Heel
steps_taught.description: Stepping on the ball of the foot and transferring weight as the heel drops.

steps_taught.name: Dig
steps_taught.description: Digging the heel into the ground.

what_works: Split-screen view showing close-up footwork alongside full body view
Slow and repetitive practice with clear counts
what_hinders: Lack of background music during the tutorial portion

quotes.text: In this tutorial, I'm going to break down some beginner tap steps.
All you're doing is picking up your toes and dropping them back on the floor.
Make sure that the step starts to take your weight and then the heel transfers.

evidence_segments.observation: Instructor demonstrates toe taps with a split-screen close-up of the feet.
evidence_segments.viewpoint: front and side mirror, mirrored image
evidence_segments.cannot_infer: exact weight distribution on the floor

extraction.distinctive_method: Uses a persistent split-screen format showing a close-up of the instructor's feet in synchronization with the full-body view.
